subject: Behavioral Economics
title: The Power of Defaults
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Power of Defaults usable.

hook.text: Countries with opt-out organ donation have 90%+ donor rates. Opt-in countries average 15%.

buildup.text: Defaults are the pre-selected option when you do nothing. They're the most powerful nudge because inertia is strong.

discovery.text: Johnson and Goldstein showed that defaults determine organ donation rates more than culture, religion, or education.

twist.text: Defaults work because changing requires effort, attention, and an active decision. Most people skip all three.

climax.text: Whoever sets the default effectively sets the outcome for the majority. That's enormous power.

punchline.text: The default wins. Choose it wisely.

quiz.question: Why are defaults so powerful as nudges?
options: People enjoy the default option most
Inertia means most people never change the pre-selected option
Defaults are always the best option

details.summary: Defaults are the single most powerful tool in the nudge toolkit. Whatever option is pre-selected becomes the overwhelming choice because inertia, implied endorsement, and loss aversion conspire to keep people at the starting point regardless of their actual preferences.
details.whyItMatters: Defaults determine retirement savings rates, organ donation rates, privacy settings, and consumer choices for millions. A default is not a suggestion; it is a prediction of what most people will choose.
takeaways: Most people accept defaults regardless of their stated preferences
Defaults signal an implicit recommendation from the institution setting them
The effectiveness of defaults comes from inertia, endorsement, and loss aversion

faq.question: Why are defaults more powerful than other nudges?
faq.answer: Defaults are unique because they require zero effort to accept and positive effort to reject. All other nudges compete with convenience, but defaults are convenience. The path of least resistance is always the default, and most people follow the path of least resistance.

faq.question: Should defaults always be set to the option that benefits the chooser?
faq.answer: Libertarian paternalism says yes. But defining what benefits the chooser is not always clear. For retirement savings, more is generally better. For privacy settings, preferences vary. When preferences are heterogeneous, personalized or protective defaults are appropriate.
